During a trip to Mexico in the mid-1930s, the American composer George Gershwin befriended David Alfaro Siqueiros and purchased this self-portrait. Siqueiros created the piece using non-traditional industrial cellulose nitrate paint airbrushed onto a panel coated with phenolic resin. Gershwin died in 1937, possibly without ever seeing the work, as he did not return to New York after 1936. Following his death, the painting remained quietly in the Gershwin family for eighty years. Because it had vanished from public view for so long, many presumed the artwork had been lost until it resurfaced and entered the museum collection.

credit_line: David Alfaro Siqueiros, a prominent Mexican muralist
story: David Alfaro Siqueiros created this self-portrait in 1937 at his Experimental Workshop in New York, applying cellulose nitrate automobile paint with an airbrush and drip techniques onto board coated with phenolic resin. The composer George Gershwin, who had befriended Siqueiros during a trip to Mexico, purchased the finished picture. Gershwin never returned to New York before his sudden death in July 1937, and he likely never saw the completed work. Although the portrait remained well known among art historians, the public lost track of it for eighty years while it stayed privately within the Gershwin family. In 2017, the painting resurfaced through an art dealer and entered the permanent collection of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
